paraphrase: Mad with grief, Śiva wandered eastward carrying Satī's corpse on his shoulder; since the corpse would not decay through contact with Hara's body, Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śani entered it invisibly by yogic power and let it fall piece by piece: the two feet first at Devīkūṭa, the thighs at Uḍḍīyāna, the circle of the yoni at Kāmagiri in Kāmarūpa (and the navel there too), the breasts with their golden necklace at Jālandhara, the shoulders and neck at Pūrṇagiri, the head beyond; other small parts were carried by the wind to the heavenly Gaṅgā; wherever a part fell, Mahādeva himself stayed there in the form of a liṅga, bound by love for Satī, and the gods worshipped her feet and other parts.
notes: In this account the body is dismembered by Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śani entering it — not by Viṣṇu's discus, as in later popular and Bengali versions. paraphrase: The offering chapter (the 'rudhirādhyāya'): the Lord tells his sons the order of offering (bali) according to the Vaiṣṇavī Tantra; birds, tortoises, crocodiles, fish, deer, buffalo, goats and other animals — and, the text says, a man, and one's own blood — are named as offerings to Caṇḍikā and Bhairava; by offerings liberation and heaven are attained and a king conquers his enemies; the Goddess's satisfaction is said to last longer according to the victim. Restricted: summary only; no victims' order, durations or procedure are reproduced.
notes: Chapter 67 in the Vaṅgavāsī edition; often cited as ch. 71 in other editions. Translated by W. C. Blaquiere (1799) as 'The Rudhirádhyáya, or Sanguinary Chapter'. paraphrase: Restrictions on offering: a king offers a horse only in the horse sacrifice and an elephant only in its own rite; a brāhmaṇa must never offer wine to the Great Goddess; a brāhmaṇa who offers a lion, tiger or man goes to hell and in this life loses longevity and happiness; offering one's own blood incurs the sin of self-slaughter; by offering wine a brāhmaṇa falls from brāhmaṇa status; kṣatriyas and others must not offer the black antelope.
